summaries.gardner: Chevron has strong recent momentum (shares up about 46% in a year) and an experienced management team, but it is a mature commodity producer, not the top dog in an emerging industry, and it lacks a brand-led, hard-to-copy advantage. It fits few of the Rule Breaker traits.
summaries.buffett: Chevron is simple to understand, conservatively financed and has been a Berkshire holding, but its earnings swing with oil prices (a $5,543M loss in 2020, $35,465M profit in 2022, $12,299M in 2025). Returns on capital of about 8% are ordinary, and at about 21 times trailing earnings there is no clear margin of safety; Berkshire cut its stake by about 35% in Q1 2026.
summaries.munger: Munger would respect Chevron's capital discipline and low-cost Permian, Tengiz and Guyana barrels, but would note it sells a commodity at prices it cannot set. Inverting, the main ways to lose are an oil-price collapse, long-term demand decline, political risk in places like Kazakhstan and Venezuela, and climate litigation.
summaries.lynch: Chevron is a cyclical in Lynch's terms, and he warned that cyclicals look cheapest near peak earnings: its forward P/E of about 12 rests on 2026's oil spike, with consensus EPS falling from about $17 in 2026 to about $14.9 in 2027. The share count rose about 12% after the Hess deal and insiders have been selling, not buying.
summaries.fisher: Chevron scores on Fisher's points for long-range planning, cost control and depth of engineering, but it sells undifferentiated products with no special selling edge and an operating margin of about 13%. Its growth comes more from acquisitions and commodity prices than from new products.
summaries.graham: Chevron passes Graham's tests for size, financial strength (current ratio 1.25, debt about 19% of equity) and dividend record (39 straight years of increases). It fails on earnings stability (a 2020 loss) and price: about 24 times 2023-2025 average EPS and a P/E times P/B of about 47.
summaries.thiel: Chevron does not fit Thiel's monopoly-through-technology view: it competes with Exxon, Shell, Aramco and others in a global commodity market. Its Guyana and Tengiz stakes are valuable resources, but not proprietary 10x technology.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner favours secular growth compounders with clear catalysts; Chevron's 2026 gains came from an oil-price spike and analysts expect revenue to fall in 2027 and 2028. The Microsoft data-center power project adds an AI angle, but it is small and not yet approved.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller trades macro themes and price momentum, and Chevron has both in 2026: Middle East supply disruption pushed Brent to $104 in Q2 and the shares rose about 46% in a year. The thesis depends on oil staying high, so it fits as a macro trade rather than a long-term compounder.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical, capital-heavy businesses with modest returns and no pricing power, and Chevron's ROIC of about 8% and operating margin of about 13% fall short of his bar. It would not qualify as a 'good company' under his rules.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Chevron is middling: ROIC is about 8% and EV/EBIT of about 16.7 gives an earnings yield near 6%. Neither measure would rank it near the top.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, great people and great reinvestment; Chevron has capable management and reinvests in the Permian, Guyana and Tengiz, but its commodity business earns ordinary returns on that capital. It fits one leg rather than all three.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai buys simple businesses in temporary distress at deep discounts; Chevron was such a case in 2020, but today it trades near record highs after the 2026 oil spike. Low debt limits downside, but the price is not a bargain.
summaries.wood: Chevron is the opposite of ARK's disruptive-innovation focus, which expects electric vehicles and batteries to erode oil demand. Its lithium, renewable fuels and data-center power projects are small next to oil and gas.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with pricing power; Chevron produces large cash flows (about $27.0B TTM free cash flow) but has no pricing power and unpredictable earnings. It does not fit his core criteria.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared model does not fit a price taker: Chevron's scale lowers its costs, but the savings are kept as margin rather than passed to customers to build loyalty. Its future depends on oil prices more than on deepening a moat.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing markets and products that solve painful problems; Chevron supplies essential energy but in a mature market whose revenue fell from $246,252M in 2022 to $189,031M in 2025. It is far from the kind of opportunity Sequoia backs.
summaries.nash: Chevron fails most of Nash's 12-step screens: it is a commodity producer (a zone to avoid), carries more debt ($37,075M) than cash ($8,530M), has an operating margin of about 13% and has no consistent revenue growth. It does pass the banker's lending test and has beaten recent earnings estimates, but scores about 65 of 130 on his categories.

momentum.evidence: CVX rose about 46% in the 52 weeks to mid-October 2026 (to about $220) and about 36% in 2026 to early October, well ahead of the S&P 500.

g4.evidence: CEO Mike Wirth is a respected operator and Berkshire Hathaway still held about 84.3 million shares after Q1 2026, but Berkshire cut its stake by about 35% that quarter.

g6.evidence: After the 2026 rally some commentators (for example TIKR, estimating about 0.6% annual return to 2030) see CVX as fully valued, though its forward P/E of about 12 is not called extreme.

simple.evidence: Chevron produces oil and gas, refines fuels and sells them, a business a careful generalist can follow.

b2.evidence: Results swing with commodity prices: a $5,543M loss in 2020, $35,465M net income in 2022 and $12,299M in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Management reports candidly and has a long record of dividends and disciplined spending, but insiders sold about $581M of stock in the past year, including Wirth's $63.6M in August 2026, and it faces climate lawsuits.

b6.evidence: Noble (2020), PDC (2023) and Hess (2025) fit its core strategy, though the deals also reflect the industry's consolidation race.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 8% and ROE about 12% with modest debt (debt/equity 0.19), adequate but neither high nor consistent across the cycle.

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $16,592M on net income of $12,299M, and TTM free cash flow was about $27.0B on net income of $20.59B.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded growth in the Permian, Tengiz and Hess, and the stock has roughly doubled since 2021, but it went nowhere from 2014 to 2020.

safety.evidence: At about $220, roughly 21 times trailing earnings and near record highs, the price offers no margin of safety against a fall in oil prices.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 12 looks reasonable, but it rests on 2026 oil prices; analysts expect EPS to fall about 12% in 2027.

mu5.evidence: A 16.3% debt ratio and low-cost assets make failure unlikely, but oil price collapses, energy transition, country risk and climate policy are several plausible ways to lose value.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in the Permian, Guyana (Hammerhead approved) and Tengiz at decent returns, but returns depend on oil prices and reserves deplete.

ly2.evidence: Chevron is a classic cyclical whose story is volume growth from Hess, the Permian and Tengiz plus cost cuts and dividends.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 21 is well above its long-run earnings growth; EPS fell from $18.28 in 2022 to $6.63 in 2025 before the 2026 spike.

runway.evidence: Revenue (total revenues and other income) was $189,031M in 2025, below 2022's $246,252M, and analysts expect about $215.9B in 2028, below 2026's estimate.

ly7.evidence: Insiders sold about $581M of stock in the past 12 months with no purchases, and diluted shares rose about 12% year on year after the Hess deal despite buybacks.

ly8.evidence: CVX is one of the largest and most widely followed US stocks, covered by about 25 analysts.

fi2.evidence: It is developing power for data centers, lithium, renewable fuels and carbon capture, but these are small next to oil and gas.

fi3.evidence: Technology improves drilling and recovery in the Permian and deepwater, but new products add little revenue so far.

fi4.evidence: Oil, gas and fuels are sold largely on price, so selling skill is not a distinctive advantage.

longterm.evidence: Management invests through the cycle in multi-decade projects such as Tengiz, Australian LNG and Guyana and kept raising the dividend through 2020.

gr1.evidence: Chevron has a market value of about $427B and 2025 total revenues of $189,031M.

ni10.evidence: It reported net losses in 2020 ($5,543M) and 2016.

gr4.evidence: Chevron has paid dividends for decades and raised them for 39 consecutive years; the current quarterly rate is $1.78.

eps10.evidence: Net income rose from about $4.6B in 2015 to $12,299M in 2025 (diluted EPS $6.63), more than a one-third gain per share.

gr6.evidence: The price of about $220 is about 24 times average 2023-2025 diluted EPS ($11.36, $9.72, $6.63).

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 20.9 times a P/B of about 2.25 gives about 47, above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its technology is strong but not ten times better than Exxon's, Shell's or Aramco's.

timing.evidence: 2026 Middle East supply disruption lifted oil prices and AI data centers boost gas demand, but long-term oil demand faces electrification.

th3.evidence: Chevron is a 140-year-old incumbent in a huge, mature market, not a company that started by dominating a niche.

team.evidence: Wirth's team is seasoned and closed Hess despite Exxon's arbitration challenge, but it is a professional rather than exceptional founder team.

th5.evidence: Its refineries, Chevron and Texaco stations, LNG contracts and trading arm give it reliable outlets for its production.

durable.evidence: Low-cost, long-life resources should keep it among the leaders for decades, but oil demand may decline over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Its Hess deal secured 30% of Guyana's Stabroek block, a unique resource, but the opportunity was widely known.

trend.evidence: It is not an AI or cloud leader, though its planned 2.67 GW gas-fired plant for a Microsoft data center taps AI power demand.

dr1.evidence: TTM EPS rose to about $10.41 from $6.63 in 2025, Q2 2026 net income was $12,072M and 2026 consensus EPS is about $17, though 2027 estimates are lower.

dr2.evidence: Hess synergies ($1.5B run rate), record production and cost cuts should help, but oil prices may fall from 2026 levels.

dr4.evidence: Middle East supply disruption favours it now, but a slowing economy or easing of the conflict could push oil prices back down.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include Q3 results on October 30, 2026, a final decision on the Microsoft power project by end-2026, more Guyana FPSOs and Tengiz ramp-up.

dr7.evidence: It could be a large position for an oil-bull macro view, but dependence on commodity prices limits conviction.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is about 44% but operating margin is about 13%, typical of a commodity business without pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: Free-cash-flow yield is about 6.3% (about $27.0B TTM FCF on a $427B market value), attractive though flattered by high oil prices.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 16.7, an operating earnings yield of about 6%.

pa2.evidence: The industry is in an upswing driven by the 2026 oil-price spike, not a temporary setback.

pa4.evidence: Low debt and long-life assets limit permanent loss for the company, but buying near record highs after an oil spike carries real price risk.

wo1.evidence: Chevron is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics, though it is exploring lithium and data-center power.

wo2.evidence: Oil and gas production costs are not falling fast enough to open large new demand.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several ARK-style innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market will not be many times larger in five years; analysts expect revenue to decline after 2026.

ac3.evidence: Earnings depend heavily on oil, gas and refining margins, as the jump from $2,490M of Q2 2025 net income to $12,072M in Q2 2026 shows.

ns1.evidence: As a price taker, it keeps scale savings as margin rather than sharing them with customers to widen a moat.

ns4.evidence: Hess, Guyana and the Permian strengthen its cost position, but long-term oil demand makes a clearly stronger position in 10-20 years uncertain.

va2.evidence: It supplies fuels and gas that billions of people need for transport, heating and power.

tn1.evidence: Chevron is a 140-year-old oil producer retrofitting into data-center power and lithium, not a company built for a secular trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees an oil major; its gas-to-power business for AI data centers is a possible new story but still small and unapproved.

tn3.evidence: It is a commodity producer, one of Nash's zones to avoid.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable, but revenue fell in 2023 and 2025 and debt ($37,075M) exceeds cash ($8,530M), so it passes only one of three.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive each quarter, but debt has exceeded cash in every recent quarter (e.g., $40,758M vs $6,293M at end-2025).

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of -6.8% in 2025 plus a free-cash-flow margin of 8.8% is about 2, and even TTM figures (about 7% growth plus 12.9% FCF margin) total about 20, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: TTM operating income rose to about $27.2B from $17.6B in 2025, so revenue grew faster than operating expenses over the last year.

tn9.evidence: It hits instant kills: debt exceeds cash and the operating margin of about 13% is below 20%.

tn10.evidence: It faces climate lawsuits from Honolulu and California and political risk in Venezuela and Kazakhstan.

tn11.evidence: Chevron provides oil, gas and fuels that help drivers, airlines, utilities and factories run, and charges market prices per barrel, cubic foot or gallon.

tn13.evidence: Total about 65 of 130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest 10 (1.3%), institutional ownership 10 (71%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 10, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 0, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in 2023 and 2025, margins did not expand steadily, and debt exceeded cash in every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 19x, assets excluding goodwill ($325,567M) are 2.4x liabilities ($134,577M), the current ratio is 1.25 and liabilities are 0.69x equity.

tn18.evidence: Wirth has executed well since 2018 (Noble, PDC, Hess, record output), but he sold about $63.6M of shares in August 2026 rather than buying, and he is not a founder.

tn20.evidence: Chevron beat adjusted EPS estimates in Q1 and Q2 2026; Q2 adjusted EPS was $6.06 versus a $5.55 estimate.

tn21.evidence: Insiders sold heavily during the 2026 rally (director John Hess about $157M and Wirth about $63.6M in August), and margins have been volatile.

tn22.evidence: It has large revenue, solid profits and buys back stock rather than selling it.

tn24.evidence: A 6.3% free-cash-flow yield implies only low-single-digit growth, but that free cash flow is inflated by 2026 oil prices and revenue fell from 2022 to 2025.

tn25.evidence: With 3-year averages of about -8.1% revenue growth and an 8.7% FCF margin, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate, value is about $50 a share, far below about $220.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 12 is in line with Exxon but above TotalEnergies (about 7) and Equinor (about 9), and with 2027 EPS expected to fall, the forward PEG is not below 1.
